newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG soldiers free defence chief from house arrest.
newsitem.headline: PNG soldiers free defence chief from house arrest.

text.p: Papua New Guinea soldiers on Monday freed the country's defence chief from house arrest after the Pacific nation's new prime minister agreed to suspend charges against troops involved in an army revolt in March.
"We are implementing the prime minister's directive (to release the commander) straight away and I expect the other party to honour its commitment," Major Walter Enuma told reporters.
"I think under the circumstances...it is a very bold move and a very amicable solution at this point in time," he said.

Defence Force commander Brigadier Colonel Leo Nuia had been held under house arrest all day in his residence inside Murray Barracks, the country's army headquarters. A special forces unit armed with rocket launchers had guarded Nuia.
Soldiers detained Nuia on Monday morning after earlier freeing Enuma from a police cell where he was awaiting a court appearance on firearm charges related to the June election.
The soldiers had demanded a general amnesty for all troops involved in a March revolt against 70 African mercenaries hired to end the secessionist rebellion on Bougainville island.
Local media have reported that the commander of the revolt, former Brigadier General Jerry Singirok, will be charged with sedition on Tuesday.
Enuma was Singirok's right-hand man and commanded the operation to throw the mercenaries out of the South Pacific nation, which resulted in two days of looting and mass protests.
Prime Minister Bill Skate earlier said he could not meet the soldiers' demand for an amnesty, but agreed to suspend the rebellion-related charges and re-open a mercenary inquiry.

Skate said he had directed the police commissioner and attorney general to "withhold all charges" pending a new inquiry into the US$36 million mercenary deal with British military consultant Sandline International.
Skate said he now "pleaded for calm and understanding" from the defence force, pending the mercenary inquiry.

"The prime minister has therefore appealed for the members of the defence force to give his government a chance to be fully briefed on the Sandline crisis and for the inquiry to be completed before the government can make clear and considered decisions in relation to those people involved," Skate said.
In March, Papua New Guinea was rocked by its worst crisis since independence in 1975, when the army revolted against the hiring of mercenaries to end the Bougainville conflict.
The revolt sparked two days of looting and mass protests in the capital Port Moresby which forced the then prime minister Sir Julius Chan to step down.

A judicial inquiry into the mercenary deal cleared Chan of any wrongdoing and he returned to office within weeks of the election. But a voter backlash against political corruption and the mercenary deal saw more than 50 politicians, including Chan, lose their seats.
A new government, which included the former ruling coalition parties, was formed last week, headed by prime minister Skate, who campaigned against the mercenary deal and corruption.
